## What it is

Gelman's example is copy editors. Checking an article about to appear in a statistics journal, he found that the copy editor "had made a bunch of stupid changes that I then had to go back and fix", and the same had happened with his books. How can professional editors do worse than a statistician, "for whom writing is only a small part of the job description"? His answer is the pinch-hitter syndrome. As a kid he assumed pinch hitters must be the best sluggers in baseball, "because all they do (well, almost all) is hit. But of course this isn't the case—the best hitters play outfield, or first base, or third base, or whatever. If the pinch hitter were really good, he'd be a starter."

He ends with a question rather than an answer: "There must be some general social-science principle here, about generalists and specialists, roles in an organization, etc?" The other examples and the mechanisms on this page are our suggestions.

## Why it matters

Organizations often handle quality by assigning a specialist: a proofreader, a methods reviewer, a compliance officer. The pinch-hitter syndrome warns that this can create false confidence. The specialist may have been selected for availability rather than skill, may lack the surrounding context that makes the task go well, and may not get the steady practice that keeps generalists sharp.

## How it works

Several mechanisms may combine. Gelman's post points to the first, selection. The other two are our suggestions, and the simulation shows the first two.

1. **Selection.** The best hitters play every day. The bench, where pinch hitters come from, has players who weren't good enough to start.
2. **Lack of rhythm or context.** Coming in cold for one at-bat (or one proofreading pass at the end of a project) is harder than being involved throughout.
3. **Narrow incentives.** A person rewarded for one narrow output may optimize what is checked, not what matters.

## Simulated example

A league has 400 hitters with true talent spread around a .260 batting average. The best players start. Pinch hitters come from the remaining players and also face a "cold start" penalty. Compare the batting averages.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, mean, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof starterShare = Inputs.range([0.3, 0.9], {value: 0.6, step: 0.05, label: "Share of players who start"})
viewof coldPenalty = Inputs.range([0, 0.04], {value: 0.015, step: 0.005, label: "Cold-start penalty"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 8, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
pinch = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const players = range(400).map(i => ({i, talent: Math.min(0.36, Math.max(0.17, r.normal(0.26, 0.025)))}))
    .sort((a, b) => b.talent - a.talent);
  const nStart = Math.round(starterShare * players.length);
  return players.map((p, k) => {
    const role = k < nStart ? "Starter" : "Pinch hitter";
    const atBats = role === "Starter" ? 500 : 60;
    const p0 = role === "Starter" ? p.talent : p.talent - coldPenalty;
    return {...p, role, avg: r.binomial(atBats, p0) / atBats};
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "The Pinch-Hitter Syndrome: simulation chart",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: Season batting average. Vertical axis: Players. The chart updates with the controls above it, and the summary below the charts states the result in words.",
  height: 280,
  x: {label: "Season batting average", domain: [0.1, 0.4]},
  y: {grid: true, label: "Players"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Starter", "Pinch hitter"], range: ["#2166ac", "#d6604d"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(pinch, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: "avg", fill: "role", fillOpacity: 0.6, mixBlendMode: "multiply", thresholds: 40})),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const m = role => mean(pinch.filter(d => d.role === role).map(d => d.avg));
  const t = role => mean(pinch.filter(d => d.role === role).map(d => d.talent));
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`Starters hit **${fmt(m("Starter"), 3)}** and pinch hitters hit **${fmt(m("Pinch hitter"), 3)}**. Of that gap, **${fmt(t("Starter") - t("Pinch hitter"), 3)}** comes from selection alone (difference in true talent). The rest comes from the cold-start penalty and luck. The specialists are worse at their only job.`}</div>`;
}
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Specialization does not guarantee competence. Ask how the specialist was selected.
- A single check from someone coming in cold is a weak safeguard. Quality is better built in throughout.
- When comparing groups, separate selection effects from the effect of the role itself.
:::
